entry.evidence: their potential for nitrate removal is yet to be investigated

steps.action: Pose the question of how bacterial and archaeal community composition varies with depth alongside groundwater geochemistry and isotopes in the nitrate-contaminated Abbotsford-Sumas aquifer.
steps.quote: In this study, we investigated groundwater geochemistry and the composition of bacterial and archaeal communities with increasing depth

steps.action: Take from earlier work the position that the aquifer has little denitrification capacity, restricted to deep localized pockets and riparian zones.
steps.quote: denitrification is therefore thought to be restricted to localized pockets deeper in the aquifer

steps.action: Take from the literature the isotopic expectations of denitrification (residual nitrate enriched in 15N and 18O) and of sulfide-coupled denitrification (low δ34S and δ18O of sulfate).
steps.quote: the residual nitrate pool becomes enriched in heavy isotopes

steps.action: Name two-end-member groundwater mixing as the rival that can mimic the isotopic signatures of denitrification, and motivate DNA-based community analysis as an extra line of evidence.
steps.quote: mixing between groundwater from two end member sources

steps.action: Analyse decade-long anion records (ECCC data) and five-year nitrate isotope records from wells 91-15 and 91-13 by linear regression, finding decreasing nitrate and chloride and increasing sulfate in the deeper well.
steps.quote: both NO3-N and Cl− decreased significantly (p < 0.001)

steps.action: State three rivals for the deep-well trends: land-use change in the capture zone, biological nitrate removal, and mixing of two water types; none is singled out.
steps.quote: suggest either changes in agricultural practices in the capture zone, and/or varying degrees of biological nitrate removal and/or mixing

steps.action: Deploy a passive diffusion sampler (design from Malekani et al., 2018) with 10-cm ports for 30 days in the fully screened well ABB-14 and profile major ions, DO, Fe(II), TIC, TOC and nitrate and sulfate isotopes from 4 to 20 mbgs, finding a 2-m redoxcline at 18–20 mbgs.
steps.quote: A redoxcline was further observed within a 2 m transition zone at 18–20 mbgs characterized by sharp declines in nitrate concentrations

steps.action: Check sampler equilibration with a bromide tracer preloaded in each vial and exclude vials with Br− above 0.5 mg/L (Methods).
steps.quote: were excluded from subsequent analyses

steps.action: Resample four discrete depths in ABB-14 with paired packers in June 2018 and find the vertical chemistry trend consistent with the November 2016 diffusion profile.
steps.quote: The vertical trend in water chemistry was more or less consistent

steps.action: Compare the profiles with the rivals: declining conservative chloride with rising sulfate and TIC indicates mixing below 16 mbgs, while DO and Fe(II) shifts at 18–20 mbgs indicate a redox change allowing nitrate respiration; the authors name this interval the nitrate depletion zone (NDZ).
steps.quote: altogether suggest [...] shallow and deep groundwater [...] at 16 mbgs and below

steps.action: Compare the δ15N and δ18O excursions of nitrate and the sharp δ34S-sulfate decrease in the NDZ with the expected signatures of denitrification coupled to sulfur oxidation.
steps.quote: The above isotopic signatures support the occurrence of microbial respiration of nitrate

steps.action: Note that the 2018 packer samples show a similar vertical pattern of nitrate isotope values in the NDZ, extending to 19.5 mbgs.
steps.quote: A similar vertical trend of decreasing nitrate isotope values in the NDZ was observed in the samples

steps.action: Address the mismatch that the strongest isotopic evidence comes from water that is not fully anoxic by relaxing the anoxia auxiliary, citing work showing nitrate respiration under suboxic conditions.
steps.quote: completely anoxic conditions were not mandatory for anaerobic nitrate respiration to occur in natural systems

steps.action: Sequence bacterial and archaeal 16S rRNA gene amplicons from eight depths (DADA2 ASVs, SILVA taxonomy) and check coverage with species accumulation curves.
steps.quote: High-throughput sequencing of 16S rRNA gene amplicon libraries from eight samples representing discreet groundwater depths

steps.action: Run DNA extraction and PCR reagent blanks, which show no amplification (Methods, p. 4); confirm lower bacterial richness in the NDZ with two statistical tests, pairwise Wilcoxon and ANOVA with Tukey (p. 6).
steps.quote: No amplification was observed when DNA extraction blanks or nuclease free water (PCR reagent blank) was used as templates

steps.action: Describe phylum and order distributions with depth: Omnitrophicaeota, Patescibacteria and Rokubacteria decline with depth, Nitrososphaeria are abundant in shallow samples, and Proteobacteria and Acidiferrobacterales are enriched within and below the NDZ.
steps.quote: Omnitrophicaeota, Patescibacteria and Rokubacteria diminished with increasing depth

steps.action: Compare bacterial communities across the three depth groups by PCoA of weighted UniFrac distances: the NDZ communities cluster apart from those above and below, while archaeal communities show no depth clustering.
steps.quote: the NDZ harbored significantly dissimilar bacterial communities

steps.action: Test the NDZ dissimilarity with two independent statistics, PERMANOVA with FDR correction and ANOSIM, which agree.
steps.quote: (PERMANOVA pseudoF = 2.08, p.adj = 0.013, 999 permutations; ANOSIM R = 0.63, P = 0.039)

steps.action: Relate community structure to water chemistry by BIOENV and canonical correspondence analysis: TIC and nitrate isotope values align with the NDZ communities.
steps.quote: strongly influenced the microbial community structure within the NDZ compared to shallower and deeper groundwater

steps.action: Find that Sulfurifustis, Sulfuritalea, Sulfuricella and Gallionella peak at 19–19.5 mbgs and correlate with δ15N-NO3− (Pearson; Fig. 6, p. 9).
steps.quote: peaking at 19–19.5 mbgs within the NDZ

steps.action: Compare the genera with published physiology, genomes and nirS surveys, and place the NDZ ASVs on a PhyML/ARB tree next to sequences from denitrifying systems, concluding that the genera are consistent with sulfur-oxidizing denitrification.
steps.quote: their potential involvement in biological nitrate removal coupled to the oxidation of inorganic sulfur compounds in the ASA

steps.action: Raise, as an open possibility, that Gallionella performs lithotrophic nitrate-dependent Fe(II) oxidation in the NDZ, while noting that nitrate reduction is not shown to be conserved in Gallionellaceae.
steps.quote: is particularly intriguing in this regard in terms of lithotrophic nitrate-dependent iron oxidation

steps.action: Interpret the Desulfosporosinus peak at 20 mbgs, where sulfate is high, as sulfate reducers fed by biologically produced sulfate from above, possibly growing autotrophically on hydrogen, giving a stratified nitrate–sulfate redox sequence.
steps.quote: the supply of biologically produced sulfate from above can explain the colonization of Desulfosporosinus at the bottom of the NDZ

steps.action: Keep the claim that the ordered stratification of nitrate reducers above sulfate reducers, consistent with the geochemistry and isotopes, supports denitrification potential at the sampled location; mixing is retained, not excluded, and no mixing model or enrichment factor is computed.
steps.quote: providing additional support for the potential of denitrification

tree.answer: A 2-m nitrate depletion zone (redoxcline) at 18–20 mbgs
Nitrate loss is observed; denitrification is inferred from isotopes and taxa
Identify microbial key players and tie nitrate removal to the sampled location
Denitrification (sulfur-coupled) versus two-end-member mixing; land-use change for long-term trends
Partly: chloride separates mixing, but isotopes are not unique under mixing
Conditions found in the aquifer; one well profiled
Consistent across 2016 and 2018; paired statistics agree
Denitrification supported as best explanation alongside mixing

end.claim: In a 2-m nitrate depletion zone at 18–20 mbgs, nitrate isotope excursions, a δ34S decrease and a stratified community of putative sulfur-oxidizing denitrifiers above sulfate reducers support sulfur-coupled denitrification at the sampled location, alongside mixing of shallow and deep groundwater.

decisive_move.sentence: The 10-cm-resolution passive diffusion profile in the fully screened well revealed the 2-m nitrate depletion zone that every later geochemical, isotopic and microbial comparison targets.

gates.evidence: Action: no stated hypothesis directed the 2016 diffusion sampling, which used an existing sampler (p. 3). The 2018 packer resampling targeted NDZ depths (p. 3), but no reason tied to a hypothesis is given. Claim: the isotopes could have failed to show enrichment, and the NDZ community could have failed to differ (PERMANOVA and ANOSIM). However, mixing was never excluded, and the authors state the data could not separate mixing from local denitrification (p. 11). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing on Illumina MiSeq with Klindworth primers
DADA2 ASV inference, Cutadapt, SILVA 138 taxonomy
Weighted UniFrac, PCoA, PERMANOVA, ANOSIM, BIOENV, CCA (phyloseq, vegan)
MAFFT, FastTree, SINA, ARB, PhyML maximum-likelihood trees
Known lithoautotrophic sulfur-oxidizing and nitrate-reducing metabolism of Sulfurifustis, Sulfuritalea, Sulfuricella; sulfate reduction by Desulfosporosinus

novelty_claims.quote: their potential for nitrate removal is yet to be investigated
has not been widely used in groundwater nitrate studies.

limits:
No peer-review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The XML text contains only the abstract and captions, so body steps cite printed pages.

What the process does not show:
- Mixing is invoked but not quantified. The authors state the data were insufficient for an enrichment factor or a two-end-member mixing model, and that they could not tell whether denitrification occurred at the sampled location or elsewhere (p. 11). This sits in tension with the abstract's claim that the stratification 'connects nitrate removal to the locations of the aquifer sampled' (§0 ¶1).
- Microbial evidence rests on eight samples (two or three per depth group) from one profile. It consists of taxon presence and correlation, with no functional genes, rates or activity measurements.
- The archaeal communities showed no depth clustering.
- The decade-long data were provided by ECCC, not collected here.

Internal inconsistencies:
- The well depths for 91-15 and 91-14 are swapped between the Fig. 1 caption and the text and Fig. 2. Well 91-13 is given as 20.0, 20.9 and >20 mbgs in different places.
- The abstract calls Desulfosporosinus 'putative heterotrophic' sulfate reducers, while p. 10 argues they may grow autotrophically on hydrogen.

Sub-claim statuses (my reading):
- Mixing below 16 mbgs: best_explanation (the authors say chloride changes 'confirm' it).
- NDZ bacterial community distinct from those above and below: confirmed by PERMANOVA and ANOSIM, in a small sample.
- Gallionella nitrate-dependent Fe(II) oxidation: hypothesis only, status none.
- Long-term trends in well 91-13: no conclusion among three rivals.

Codings that are my inference:
- Steps 2 to 4 are cited framing taken from the Introduction.
- Treating the 2018 resampling as replication is my reading; the paper presents it as a follow-up campaign.

disagreements.target: Wassenaar (1995): the aquifer has little intrinsic capacity for biological nitrate removal
disagreements.support: Isotopic excursions, a δ34S decrease and enriched putative sulfur-oxidizing denitrifiers in the 18–20 mbgs NDZ indicate local denitrification potential. This is consistent with denitrification confined to deeper pockets (Tesoriero et al., 2000; Wassenaar et al., 2006).
disagreements.quote: this aquifer has little intrinsic capacity

disagreements.target: Earlier view that groundwater denitrification depends on bioavailable organic matter and heterotrophy (Khan and Spalding, 2004; Korom, 1992)
disagreements.support: No TOC change across the NDZ, rising TIC, a δ34S-sulfate decrease and abundant lithoautotrophic sulfur oxidizers point to sulfur-coupled lithotrophic denitrification, in line with the recent studies the authors cite.
disagreements.quote: was previously thought to be heavily dependent on bioavailable organic matter

disagreements.target: He et al. (2016): narG-encoded nitrate reduction potential in an autotrophic Gallionellaceae Fe(II) oxidizer
disagreements.support: The authors note that no other cultured Gallionellaceae have been shown to reduce nitrate, so the genetic potential cannot be generalized to the family. They nonetheless find the Gallionella–isotope correlation intriguing.
disagreements.quote: cannot be taken as a conserved feature within

alternatives_considered.chosen: None singled out; all three kept open
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Land-use change in the capture zone (raspberry to blueberry); biological nitrate removal; mixing of shallow high-solute and deep low-solute groundwater
alternatives_considered.reason: Groundwater age increasing with depth supports possible mixing; no test separates the rivals

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Seasonal changes in biological nitrate removal as the cause of high δ15N-NO3− events in well 91-13
alternatives_considered.reason: The δ18O-NO3− values did not follow the δ15N increase in the same sampling events

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both mixing (below 16 mbgs) and nitrate respiration (18–20 mbgs) contribute
alternatives_considered.reason: Conservative chloride declines indicate mixing; DO, Fe(II) and isotope shifts indicate a redox change and nitrate respiration

alternatives_considered.chosen: TIC, NO3-N, δ15N-NO3−, δ18O-NO3− and δ34S-SO42− as CCA constraining variables
alternatives_considered.alternatives: All other subsets of water chemistry parameters tested by BIOENV
alternatives_considered.reason: Strongest Spearman correlation with bacterial community similarity (0.448)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Desulfosporosinus need not compete for organic substrates (possible autotrophic growth on hydrogen)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Competition with nitrate reducers for organic substrates, as in organic-rich habitats such as oil reservoirs
alternatives_considered.reason: Some species, including D. lacus, grow autotrophically on hydrogen; TIC increases between 16 and 20 mbgs
